# Voice Design

> Create a voice from a written description, audition it, and convert it into a voice you can use everywhere

Voice Design creates natural, realistic voices from a text description.
Describe the character you want for your voice agent or product, and Gradium
generates a few candidates. You listen, then convert the one you like into a
permanent voice. From then on it works like any other `voice_id`: REST,
WebSocket and Speech-to-Speech. No reference audio is needed.

<Card title="Have a recording instead?" icon="microphone" href="/guides/voices/custom-voices">
  Custom voices clone a speaker from a short audio sample.
</Card>

## How it works

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="1. Generate" icon="wand-magic-sparkles">
    Send a description, get candidate voices back in seconds.
  </Card>

  <Card title="2. Listen" icon="headphones">
    Audition each candidate on a short line of Text-to-Speech.
  </Card>

  <Card title="3. Convert" icon="bookmark">
    Promote your pick to a permanent `voice_id`.
  </Card>

  <Card title="4. Use it" icon="waveform-lines">
    Text-to-Speech, streaming, and Speech-to-Speech all accept it.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Describe the voice in one or two sentences, up to 500 characters, in English,
French, Spanish, Portuguese or German. Gradium expands the description into a
fuller specification and samples 1 to 5 complete voices from it, ready in a few
seconds. Audition each on a short line, then convert the one you want. Until you
convert it, a candidate cannot be used in production.

Two things to know. The model samples a new voice on every request, so if you
like a candidate, convert it: re-running the request will not bring it back. And
the candidates from one request are variations on one character. For a different
character, change the description.

## Access

Base URL `https://api.gradium.ai/api`, API key in the `x-api-key` header.

| Call | Endpoint |
| :- | :- |
| Generate candidates | `POST /voice-generator/generate` |
| Check readiness, or list candidates | `GET /voice-generator/embeddings` |
| Audition a candidate | `POST /post/speech/tts` |
| Convert a candidate | `POST /voices/from-embedding` |
| Delete a candidate | `DELETE /voice-generator/embeddings/{embedding_id}` |

### The `json_config` allow-list

<Warning>
  Send only `cfg_scale`. **An unknown key or out-of-range value is not rejected.** The request returns `201` and the candidates never become `ready`. Bound your polling loop and treat a timeout as a bad request.

  The usual causes: a synthesis setting such as `temp`, or `cfg_scale` outside its range.
</Warning>

## Synthesis settings

Auditioning a candidate or synthesising with a converted voice is an ordinary
TTS request, so everything in [Voice Settings](/guides/voice-settings) applies.
See [Model selection](/guides/text-to-speech#model-selection) for TTS model access.

<Callout color="#DC2626">
  **Deprecated: `cfg_coef` for TTS**

  The new TTS model ignores `cfg_coef` when synthesising with a designed voice. Remove it
  from TTS requests. `cfg_scale` still applies when generating the voice.
</Callout>

```json theme={null}
{
  "text": "Hi there, thanks so much for calling Northgate!",
  "voice_id": "vox_emb_njsiEgpj5NjHKdZc",
  "output_format": "wav",
  "only_audio": true,
  "json_config": { "temp": 0.5 }
}
```

### Temperature (`temp`)

`0.0` to `1.4`, default `0.7`.

* **Audition at the default.** `0.0` makes a lively voice sound flatter than it will in production.
* **`0.3` to `0.5`** for scripted, high-volume output where takes must match: IVR prompts, fixed announcements.
* **Default or slightly above** for conversational agents and narration.

## Supported tags

The models read plain text. Two inline tags are recognised, on candidates and
converted voices alike. **Anything else is spoken aloud as text.**

| Tag | Effect |
| - | - |
| `<break time="1.5s" />` | A pause of `0.1` to `2.0` seconds. Surround the tag with spaces. |
| `<flush>` | Emit audio for all text received so far. Only meaningful when streaming over the WebSocket. |

On a candidate, tags count toward the 100-character limit.

### Not supported

SSML is not interpreted. `<speak><prosody rate="slow">Hello there.</prosody></speak>`
produces a voice saying "speak prosody rate slow, hello there, slash prosody,
slash speak". Use these instead:

| Instead of | Use |
| - | - |
| `<prosody rate>` | `padding_bonus`, see [Speed control](/guides/voice-settings#speed-control) |
| `<prosody pitch>`, `<prosody volume>` | The description. Pitch and energy are attributes of the voice. |
| `<emphasis>` | Punctuation and sentence structure |
| `<say-as>`, `<sub>`, `<phoneme>` | [`rewrite_rules`](/guides/text-rewriting) or a [pronunciation dictionary](/api-reference/endpoint/create-pronunciation) |
| `<voice>` | A separate request with a different `voice_id` |

Markdown and HTML are read as text too. Strip formatting before sending.

## Candidate lifecycle

| | |
| - | - |
| **Retention** | Candidates are removed 30 days after generation. Converting one clears its expiry. |
| **Accumulation** | Generating never evicts earlier candidates. Holding them is free. |
| **Cleanup** | `DELETE /voice-generator/embeddings/{embedding_id}`. Always safe: a converted voice holds its own copy. Unknown id: `404`. |
| **Deleting a voice** | `DELETE /voices/{voice_id}` leaves the candidate intact, with no expiry. It can be converted again. |
| **Lost an id** | `GET /voice-generator/embeddings` lists every candidate, newest first, with its description. Page with `skip` and `limit` (1 to 1000, default 100). `expires_at: null` marks converted candidates. |

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
| - | - |
| Description | 1 to 500 characters |
| Candidates per request | 1 to 5, default 1 |
| Audition text | 100 characters, REST only |
| Languages | `en`, `fr`, `es`, `pt`, `de` |
| Candidate retention | 30 days, cleared once converted |
| Converted voices | Count against the custom-voice allowance |

## Errors

Errors are `{"detail": "..."}`, except `422`, which carries a list of field errors.

| Status | Where | Meaning |
| - | - | - |
| `400` | Audition | Text over 100 characters |
| `401` | Any | Invalid or expired API key |
| `404` | Audition, delete | Unknown, not ready, or another account's id |
| `409` | Convert | Already converted, not ready, or custom-voice allowance reached. `detail` says which. |
| `422` | Generate, list | Invalid `language`, `n_samples`, `prompt` or `limit` |

A candidate that never becomes ready is almost always a `json_config` value out
of range or a key the API does not recognise. See [the
allow-list](#the-json_config-allow-list).

content.text:
Yes. Gradium calls it **Voice Design**: you write a description of the voice and it generates a new one, with no reference audio needed. But you create the voice once and then reuse it. You can't restyle the voice on each request.

**How it works** ([guide](https://docs.gradium.ai/guides/voices/voice-design.md)):
1. `POST /voice-generator/generate` with `{"prompt": "...", "language": "de", "n_samples": 3}`. The description can be up to 500 characters, and you get 1–5 candidate voices back.
2. The candidates are generated in the background and are ready in a few seconds. Check with `GET /voice-generator/embeddings?embedding_id=...`.
3. Listen to a candidate with ordinary TTS, using its id as the `voice_id`. Previews are limited to 100 characters and work over REST only.
4. `POST /voices/from-embedding` turns the one you like into a permanent `voice_id`. It then works over REST, WebSocket streaming and speech-to-speech.

**Limits that matter for using it live:**
- **Not instant.** You have to wait until the candidates are ready, and you can't use one in production until you convert it.
- **Not repeatable.** Every request produces a new voice, so sending the same prompt again won't give you the same voice back. Keep the ids you want.
- **Per-request control is small.** You only get `temp` (how varied the delivery is, 0–1.4), `padding_bonus` (speed) and rewrite rules. Pitch and energy are fixed by the description. SSML is not read, so tags like `<prosody>` get spoken aloud. The only tags it understands are `<break time="..."/>` and `<flush>`.
- **Languages:** en, fr, es, pt, de. **Italian is not supported**, which matters if you need all of SBB's languages.
- **Bad settings fail silently.** Only send `cfg_scale` (how closely it follows the description) in `json_config`. An unknown key or a value out of range still returns 201, but the candidates never become ready, so put a time limit on your status checks.
- Converted voices count toward your custom-voice limit. Unconverted candidates expire after 30 days.

For you, that means it suits designing a persona once (or once per user) and caching the `voice_id`. It doesn't suit changing the voice's character mid-conversation. For that, you'd have to switch between several voices you designed in advance.

import base64

import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

load_dotenv(HERE.parent / ".env")

class Screenshot:
    id: int
    image: bytes
    mime: str
    at: float  # time.monotonic() when received
    task: asyncio.Task | None = None  # read_screen in the background; its result is the ScreenContext

async def broadcast(msg: dict) -> None:

async def read_latest(shot: Screenshot) -> dict | None:
    """Run vision on one screenshot, tell every session, return its ScreenContext or None."""
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    screen = None
    if read_screen is None:
        log.warning("vision.py not available, screenshot %d not read", shot.id)
    else:
        try:
            if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(read_screen):
                screen = await read_screen(shot.image, shot.mime)
            else:  # a sync read_screen must not block the event loop
                screen = await asyncio.to_thread(read_screen, shot.image, shot.mime)

            log.exception("vision failed on screenshot %d", shot.id)

    log.info("screenshot %d read in %.2fs: %r", shot.id, time.monotonic() - t0, summary)

def store_screenshot(image: bytes, mime: str) -> None:
    """Keep only the latest screenshot and start reading it."""
    global latest
    if latest and latest.task:
        latest.task.cancel()  # its context is stale now
    latest = Screenshot(latest.id + 1 if latest else 1, image, mime, time.monotonic())
    latest.task = asyncio.create_task(read_latest(latest))
    log.info("screenshot %d: %d bytes %s", latest.id, len(image), mime)


async def take_screen() -> tuple[Screenshot | None, dict | None]:
    """The latest screenshot and its ScreenContext if fresh and unused (contracts § HTTP).

    The caller marks it used once its turn completes, so a turn the user interrupts
    leaves the screen for the question they ask next."""
    deadline = time.monotonic() + VISION_WAIT

            return None, None

class Session:
    def __init__(self, ws: WebSocket, handsfree: bool = False):
        self.ws = ws
        self.agent = make_agent()
        self.turns = 0
        self.stt: voice.Transcriber | None = None
        self.listener = voice.ContinuousTranscriber(self.heard_speech, self.heard_turn) if handsfree else None
        self.turn_task: asyncio.Task | None = None
        self._send_lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def send(self, msg: dict) -> None:
        async with self._send_lock:
            await self.ws.send_json(msg)

    async def state(self, state: str, label: str | None = None) -> None:
        await self.send({"type": "state", "state": state} | ({"label": label} if label else {}))

    async def run_turn(self, text: str, timings: dict[str, float] | None = None) -> None:
        self.turns += 1
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        timings = timings or {}
        await self.state("thinking")

        async def on_status(label: str) -> None:
            await self.state("searching", label)

        shot, screen = await take_screen()
        timings["vision_wait"] = time.monotonic() - t0
        t_agent = time.monotonic()
        try:
            reply = await self.agent.turn(text, screen, on_status)
        except Exception:
            log.exception("turn failed")
            await self.send({"type": "error", "message": "Sorry, something went wrong."})
            await self.state("idle")
            return
        timings["agent"] = time.monotonic() - t_agent
        if shot is not None:
            shot.used = True

        await self.send({"type": "reply", "say": reply["say"], "cards": reply["cards"]})
        if cards_to_a2ui and reply["cards"]:
            messages = cards_to_a2ui(f"reply-{self.turns}", reply["cards"])
            await self.send({"type": "a2ui", "messages": messages})
        await self.state("speaking")
        try:  # aclosing: an interrupt closes the TTS socket now, not when GC finds it
            async with contextlib.aclosing(voice.speak(reply["say"])) as chunks:
                async for chunk in chunks:
                    timings.setdefault("first_audio", time.monotonic() - t0)
                    await self.send({"type": "audio", "data": chunk})
        except Exception:
            log.exception("TTS failed")  # the reply text and cards are already on screen
        await self.send({"type": "audio_end"})
        await self.state("idle")
        timings["total"] = time.monotonic() - t0
        log.info("turn %d %r timings %s", self.turns, text, {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in timings.items()})

    async def voice_turn(self, stt: voice.Transcriber) -> None:
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        try:
            text = await stt.finish()
        except Exception:
            log.exception("STT failed")
            text = ""
        if not text:
            await self.send({"type": "error", "message": "Sorry, I didn't catch that."})
            await self.state("idle")
            return
        await self.send({"type": "transcript", "text": text})
        await self.run_turn(text, {"stt": time.monotonic() - t0})

    async def heard_speech(self) -> None:
        """Hands-free: the user's first words of a turn; talking over the mascot interrupts it."""
        await self.interrupt()
        await self.state("listening")

    async def heard_turn(self, text: str) -> None:
        """Hands-free: Gradium's VAD says the user is done."""
        await self.interrupt()
        await self.send({"type": "transcript", "text": text})
        await self.start_turn(self.run_turn(text))

    async def start_turn(self, coro) -> None:
        """One turn at a time: cancel the running one first. Turns run as tasks so the
        receive loop can still hear an interrupt."""
        await self.interrupt()
        self.turn_task = asyncio.create_task(coro)

    async def interrupt(self) -> bool:
        """Cancel the running turn: the agent call and the TTS socket. True if one was running."""
        task, self.turn_task = self.turn_task, None
        if task is None or task.done():
            return False
        task.cancel()
        try:
            await task
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            pass
        log.info("turn %d interrupted", self.turns)
        return True

    async def handle(self, msg: dict) -> None:
        kind = msg.get("type")
        if kind == "audio" and self.listener is not None and isinstance(msg.get("data"), str):
            self.listener.push(msg["data"])  # hands-free: the mic never stops, no audio_end
        elif kind == "audio" and isinstance(msg.get("data"), str):
            if self.stt is None:  # a new press; talking over the mascot interrupts it
                await self.interrupt()
                self.stt = voice.Transcriber()
                await self.state("listening")
            self.stt.push(msg["data"])
        elif kind == "audio_end" and self.stt is not None:
            stt, self.stt = self.stt, None
            await self.start_turn(self.voice_turn(stt))
        elif kind == "text" and isinstance(msg.get("text"), str):
            await self.start_turn(self.run_turn(msg["text"]))
        elif kind == "screen":
            try:
                image = base64.b64decode(msg.get("data"), validate=True)
            except (TypeError, ValueError):
                image = b""
            if msg.get("mime") in SCREEN_MIMES and 0 < len(image) <= SCREEN_MAX_BYTES:
                store_screenshot(image, msg["mime"])
            else:
                log.warning("ignored screen frame: bad mime, base64 or size")
        elif kind == "interrupt":
            if await self.interrupt():
                await self.state("idle")
        else:
            log.warning("ignored message type %r", kind)

    def close(self) -> None:
        if self.stt is not None:
            self.stt.cancel()
        if self.listener is not None:
            self.listener.cancel()
        if self.turn_task is not None:
            self.turn_task.cancel()

async def ws_endpoint(ws: WebSocket):
    await ws.accept()
    # A malformed frame: bad JSON (ValueError), a binary frame (KeyError), bad base64 (ValueError).
    # Not RuntimeError: Starlette raises it on every receive once the socket is gone.
    bad_frame = (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError)
    try:
        try:
            hello = await ws.receive_json()
        except bad_frame:
            hello = None
        if not isinstance(hello, dict) or hello.get("type") != "hello" or not token_ok(hello.get("token")):
            await ws.close(code=1008)
            return
        session = Session(ws, handsfree=hello.get("mode") == "handsfree")
        await session.agent.start()
        await session.send({"type": "ready"})
        sessions.add(session)
        try:
            while True:
                try:
                    msg = await ws.receive_json()
                    if isinstance(msg, dict):
                        await session.handle(msg)
                except bad_frame as e:
                    log.warning("ignored malformed frame: %r", e)
        finally:
            sessions.discard(session)
            session.close()
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        pass

  ```python voice_design.py theme={null}
      "A British female voice, 20 to 30, glossy and confident, with high pitch, "
      "fast pacing, high energy and bright sparkling resonance. Ideal for a "
      "friendly receptionist or assistant."
  )
  AUDITION_LINE = "Hi there, thanks so much for calling Northgate! How can I help you today?"


  def check(resp):

          raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {resp.status_code}: {resp.text}")

  def generate(prompt, language="en", n_samples=3, json_config=None):
      body = {"prompt": prompt, "language": language, "n_samples": n_samples}
      if json_config:
          body["json_config"] = json_config
      resp = check(requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/voice-generator/generate", headers=HEADERS, json=body))
      return [c["embedding_id"] for c in resp.json()["embeddings"]]


  def wait_until_ready(candidate_ids, timeout_s=120.0):
      deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout_s
      pending = set(candidate_ids)

          for candidate_id in sorted(pending):
              resp = check(requests.get(
                  f"{BASE_URL}/voice-generator/embeddings",
                  headers=HEADERS,
                  params={"embedding_id": candidate_id},
              ))
              embeddings = resp.json()["embeddings"]
              if not embeddings:
                  raise RuntimeError(f"candidate {candidate_id} not found")
              if embeddings[0]["ready"]:
                  pending.discard(candidate_id)

              time.sleep(2.0)
  ```

## Writing a description

The description is the only input the model has. It responds to the attributes a
casting brief would carry, and naming more of them gives a tighter result.

| Attribute | Examples |
| - | - |
| Gender | female, male, androgynous |
| Age | 20 to 30, middle aged, elderly |
| Accent or origin | British, Southern US, Parisian, Brazilian |
| Pitch | high pitch, deep, mid range |
| Pace | fast pacing, measured, unhurried |
| Energy | high energy, calm, subdued |
| Timbre and resonance | glossy, gravelly, breathy, bright sparkling resonance, warm |
| Register and manner | confident, girly chatter, formal, conspiratorial |
| Intended use | a friendly receptionist, an audiobook narrator, a news anchor |

End with the intended use. It steers delivery and register, not only the colour
of the voice.

> A British female voice, 20 to 30, glossy and confident, with girly
> chatter, high pitch, fast pacing, high energy and bright sparkling
> resonance. Ideal for a friendly receptionist or assistant.

### Rules of thumb

* **Use the space.** Up to 500 characters, all usable. Full sentences beat a list of adjectives.
* **Describe the voice, not the script.** Words to be spoken go in the audition line.
* **Set `language` to the language the voice will speak.** It shapes the accent and the delivery, not only the words. Regional accents still go in the description: "Bristolian" or "Parisian" has to be written out.
* **Concrete beats evaluative.** "Low pitch, slow pacing, gravelly" gives the model more than "a great narrator voice".

### Examples

| Voice | Language | Made for |
| :- | :- | :- |
| **Pirate** | English, Bristol | Character narration |
| **Fionn** | English, Ireland | Customer service |
| **Freya** | English, GB | Receptionist |
| **Desmond** | English, US | Long-form narration |

The descriptions as sent:

**Pirate**

> A gruff Bristolian English male pirate voice, 45 to 60, for game and character
> narration: weathered low pitch, gravelly timbre with heavy vocal fry, strong
> projection, at a steady, unhurried pace, boisterous and commanding energy.

**Fionn**

> An Irish English male voice, 40 to 55, for customer service: calm and crisp,
> with mid-low pitch, steady natural pacing, medium energy and warm rounded
> resonance. Ideal for reassuring walkthroughs, empathic de-escalation and
> complex IT support.

**Freya**

> A British female voice, 20 to 30, glossy and confident, with girly chatter,
> high pitch, fast pacing, high energy and bright sparkling resonance. Ideal for
> a friendly receptionist or assistant.

**Desmond**

> An American English male voice, 55 to 65: clean, deliberate and precise, with
> low pitch, slow pacing and low-to-mid energy, resonant timbre and a gentle
> low-to-high flow. Ideal for projecting academic authority.

### Iterating

Edit the attribute that is off rather than rewriting the description.

| Candidates sound... | Change |
| - | - |
| Too young or old | An explicit range: "40 to 55" rather than "middle aged" |
| Too fast or slow | "unhurried", "measured" or "fast pacing" |
| Flat | An energy word and a manner word |
| Too polished | A timbre word: "gravelly", "breathy", "weathered" |
| Right voice, wrong delivery | An intended-use clause at the end |
| Inconsistent with each other | A higher [`cfg_scale`](#cfg_scale) |

### Building this into a product

If you expose voice design to your own users, prefill a form over the
attributes above and compose the sentence from it, with a free-text box as the
escape hatch. Show the 500 character limit. Offer "keep this one" as the way to
hold onto a voice, and make regenerate send a new description rather than more
samples.

## Generation settings

Generation settings shape the voice and go in `json_config` on
`POST /voice-generator/generate`. [Synthesis settings](#synthesis-settings)
shape each utterance and go in `json_config` on the TTS request. Voice Design
still supports `cfg_scale` to control how literally the voice follows your
description.

All generation settings are optional. The defaults are tuned, so send only the
keys you have a reason to change.

```json theme={null}
{
  "prompt": "A calm Irish male voice, 40 to 55, warm and steady, for customer support.",
  "language": "en",
  "n_samples": 3,
  "json_config": { "cfg_scale": 8.0 }
}
```

| Key | Range | Default | Effect |
| - | - | - | - |
| `cfg_scale` | `1.0` to `20.0` | `5.0` | How closely the voice follows the description. Higher is more literal, less varied. |

### `cfg_scale`

* **`5.0`**, the default, when exploring with 3 to 5 candidates and you want them to differ.
* **`8.0` to `12.0`** when candidates drift from the description, or when generating one candidate at a time. Conversational designers that generate one candidate per turn typically use `10.0`.
* **Above `12.0`** the voice follows the description ever more literally at the cost of naturalness, and candidates converge on each other.

`cfg_scale` cannot add an attribute the description does not name. Fix the
[description](#writing-a-description) first.

### The `json_config` allow-list

<Warning>
  Send only `cfg_scale`. **An unknown key or out-of-range value is not rejected.** The request returns `201` and the candidates never become `ready`. Bound your polling loop and treat a timeout as a bad request.

  The usual causes: a synthesis setting such as `temp`, or `cfg_scale` outside its range.
</Warning>

content.text:
The voice-design tool works end to end against the live APIs. Asked to "talk like a grumpy old Swiss train conductor", the agent made itself that voice and then answered in it. It's committed as `a501211` on `feature/wp2-voice-design`, in the worktree `.claude/worktrees/voice-design`, branched from `origin/develop`. I haven't pushed it.

**How it works**
- **`design_voice` tool** in [dev_agent.py](backend/dev_agent.py): Gemini writes a description of the voice and the agent keeps the resulting voice for the rest of the session.
- **`voice.design_voice()`** in [voice.py](backend/voice.py): asks Gradium for one candidate voice, waits up to 30 s for it, then converts it into a permanent `voice_id`.
- **Replies carry `voice_id`**: every reply after that includes it, and [app.py](backend/app.py) passes it to `speak()`. I added it to the reply format in [contracts.md](docs/contracts.md) in the same commit.
- **CLI**: `uv run python voice.py design "<brief>"` designs a voice and writes a sample to `out.wav`.

**Tests**
- 110 offline tests pass: the 105 existing ones plus 5 new ones covering the wait-and-convert flow, the timeout, the agent tool, a failed design, and the voice reaching TTS.
- In the live run, the turn took 11.2 s:

  | Step | Time |
  | --- | --- |
  | Gemini decides to call `design_voice` | 4.3 s |
  | Gradium designs and converts the voice | 3.8 s |
  | Gemini writes the reply | 3.0 s |

  Streaming TTS in the new voice started after 0.36 s. I sent you the audio.

**Limits to know**
- **Voice slots fill up.** Each design permanently uses one of your custom-voice slots, and the code never frees them. Gradium returns a 409 error once you hit your limit. The live test used one slot, voice `YlJ3vKdMECZ965Ee`.
- **The voice doesn't persist.** It resets to the default when the WebSocket session ends.
- **Only DevAgent has the tool.** WP3's `agent.py` would need the same tool when it lands.
- **No Italian.** Gradium can only design voices in English, French, Spanish, Portuguese and German.

If repeated demos start hitting the slot limit, the fix is to delete the old voice whenever a new one replaces it.
we also need to make agent ask how user fills and then adapt/vibe voice to match the mood

Two parts: getting the agent to ask how the user feels, and changing the voice to fit the mood. Before choosing an approach, I'll check what Gradium offers for per-request tone, and how to list existing voices so mood voices can be reused.

# Voice Settings
> Fine-tune TTS output: speed, temperature, rewrite rules
TTS models accept advanced options via the `json_config` parameter. In
the Python SDK, this is a dict mapping option name to value (float or
string). For REST POST requests, pass it as an object in the JSON body.
These options apply to both the [WebSocket](/guides/text-to-speech) and
[REST](/guides/text-to-speech-rest) transports. For STT, see
[Transcription Settings](/guides/transcription-settings).
<Callout color="#DC2626">
  **Deprecated: `cfg_coef` for TTS**
  The new TTS model accepts `cfg_coef` in `json_config` but ignores its value. Remove it
  from TTS requests. Voice Design's `cfg_scale` is a separate generation setting
  and remains available.
</Callout>
## Quick reference
**Range** is the span each option is tuned and tested across.
| Parameter | Range | Default | Effect |
| - | - | - | - |
| `temp` | `0.0`–`1.4` | `0.7` | Sampling temperature. `0.0` is deterministic; higher values produce more diverse output. |
| `padding_bonus` | `-4.0`–`4.0` | `0.0` | Speech speed. Negative values are faster, positive values are slower. |
| `rewrite_rules` | string | voice language | Text-rewriting rules applied before synthesis. Defaults to the voice's language; pass `"none"` to disable. See [Text Rewriting Rules](/guides/text-rewriting). |
<Note>
  Validation accepts a wider span than the table: `temp` to `1.5`,
  `padding_bonus` from `-5.0` to `5.0`. Use the table's ranges when tuning.
</Note>
For deterministic output, set `temp` to `0.0`. For multi-utterance
flows on a single session, see [Multiplexing](/guides/multiplexing).
For designed voices, see also
[Voice Design settings](/guides/voices/voice-design#synthesis-settings).
The TTS engine recognises the `<flush>` and `<break time="..." />`
tags described in [Text-to-Speech](/guides/text-to-speech).
## Setup fields, not `json_config`
Two per-request options are set at the top level of the setup message,
alongside `voice_id`, rather than inside `json_config`:
| Field | Type | Effect |
| - | - | - |
| `pronunciation_id` | string | A pronunciation dictionary ID, applied for the whole session. See [Pronunciations](/api-reference/endpoint/list-pronunciations). |
| `model_name` | string | Model alias to synthesise with. Defaults to `default`. See [Model selection](/guides/text-to-speech#model-selection). |
`pronunciation_id` goes next to `voice_id`, at the top level of the
setup. An ID that doesn't exist is reported as `Pronunciation dictionary <id> not found.`
<Note>
  Pronunciation dictionaries apply to WebSocket sessions only. REST
  requests cannot use them; the pattern-based `rewrite_rules` in
  `json_config` are the only rewriting control there. See [Text
  Rewriting Rules](/guides/text-rewriting).
</Note>

```python theme={null}
    setup={
        "voice_id": "YTpq7expH9539ERJ",
        "output_format": "wav",
        "pronunciation_id": "bb1ckYhNHCcIJjdK",
        "json_config": {"temp": 0.3},
    },
    text="Our SDK ships today.",
)
```
## Speed control
You can guide the speed of the model using the padding bonus
parameter. Default value is 0.0. Negative values mean that the speaker
will speak faster (values between -4.0 and -0.1). Positive values mean
that the speaker will speak slower (values between 0.1 and 4.0).

The temperature for the generation can be set with values ranging from
0 to 1.4. A value of 0 corresponds to a deterministic generation, while
higher values lead to more diverse outputs. Default value is 0.7.

The agent now asks once, early in the conversation, how the user is feeling, and switches to a voice that fits their mood. It worked live with the real Gemini, SBB and Gradium. It's committed as `8946e3b` on `feature/wp2-voice-design`, not pushed.

**How it works**
- **Asking:** the prompt has the agent add "How are you feeling today?" to the end of an early answer, unless the user has already said.
- **Mood:** `respond` has a new optional `mood` field: stressed, tired (which covers sad), happy or neutral. The mood is set in the same model call as the reply, so changing the voice adds no extra Gemini call.
- **Voices:** each mood has its own voice, all built from the same mascot description: calm and slow for stressed, soft for tired, bright and fast for happy. Neutral uses the default voice. Gradium can't change tone per request, so a different mood has to be a different voice.
- **Reuse:** each mood voice is designed once and saved in your Gradium library as "Beaver mood stressed" etc. Later it's found by name in about 0.2 s, so moods only ever take three voice slots. Two are used now (stressed and happy); "tired" gets designed the first time it comes up, which adds about 4 s to that reply.

**Tests**
- 114 offline tests pass, 4 of them new for the mood flow.
- The live three-turn conversation went like this:

  | User | Agent | Time |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | "Can I make it?" | Answered with the 18:01 train, then asked how they're feeling | 9.3 s |
  | "I'm super stressed…" | Replied in the calm voice | 3.3 s |
  | "…I'm so happy" | Replied in the bright voice | 2.7 s |

- I sent you both replies as audio so you can hear the difference.

`dev_agent.py` can now take several questions as turns of one conversation, which is how I ran the live test.

**Limits to know**
- **The newest voice choice wins.** Once a "talk like a pirate" voice is set, the next mood change replaces it.
- **Mood voices only speak English well.** They were designed for English, so replies in German or French will sound off.
- **The three mood voices sound like slightly different people.** Each design produces a new speaker even from the same description.

56	## WebSocket `/ws`
57	
58	JSON text frames only, one object per frame, discriminated by `type`. Audio is base64 inside JSON. The app sends `hello` first; the server closes the socket on a wrong token.
59	
60	**App → server**
61	
62	| `type` | Fields | When |
63	| --- | --- | --- |
64	| `hello` | `token`, `mode`?: `ptt` (default) \| `handsfree` | First frame after connecting. For `handsfree`, see **Hands-free mode** below |
65	| `audio` | `data`: base64 PCM, see [Audio](#audio) | Every 80 ms while the orb is held; in hands-free mode, all the time |
66	| `audio_end` | — | Orb released; the server finalizes STT and runs the turn. Never sent in hands-free mode |
67	| `text` | `text` | Typed question (debug field); runs a turn without STT |
68	| `screen` | `mime`, `data`: base64 | Optional: an image picked in the app, for rehearsals. Same effect as `POST /screenshot` |
69	| `interrupt` | — | Tap while the mascot is talking. Stops the current turn |
70	
71	**Server → app**
72	
73	| `type` | Fields | When |
74	| --- | --- | --- |
75	| `ready` | — | After a valid `hello` |
76	| `state` | `state`: `idle` \| `listening` \| `thinking` \| `searching` \| `speaking`; `label`?: string | On every change; `label` is the tool status, e.g. "Checking trains…" |
77	| `transcript` | `text` | Final transcript of the user's turn |
78	| `reply` | `say`, `cards`: see [Cards](#cards) | Before any of the turn's audio |
79	| `a2ui` | `messages`: list of A2UI v0.9 messages, see [A2UI](#a2ui) | Right after `reply`, when it has cards |
80	| `audio` | `data`: base64 PCM | TTS chunks for the last `reply` |
81	| `audio_end` | — | TTS for the last `reply` is complete |
82	| `screen_ok` | `summary`?: string | Vision has read a new screenshot; `summary` is missing if vision failed |
83	| `error` | `message` | Turn failed; the server then sends `state: idle` |
84	
85	The orb shows `speaking` while the app still has audio queued, even after the server has sent `state: idle`.
86	
87	**Interrupting.** A new press (its first `audio` frame), a `text`, or an `interrupt` cancels the running turn: the agent call and the TTS stream. A cancelled turn sends no `audio_end`. After `interrupt` the server sends `state: idle` only if it cancelled a running turn; after a new press, `state: listening`. Gradium generates speech faster than real time, so seconds of audio may already be queued in the app. The app must stop playback the moment it interrupts, without waiting for `state: idle`, and drop `audio` frames until the next `reply`.
88	
89	**Hands-free mode.** Opt in with `"mode": "handsfree"` in `hello`; push-to-talk stays the default. The app streams `audio` for as long as it is connected, also while the mascot speaks, and never sends `audio_end`, so echo cancellation must be on (see [Audio](#audio)) or the mascot hears itself and cuts itself off. The server keeps one Gradium STT session open per connection and ends a turn with Gradium's semantic VAD: `inactivity_prob` at the 2 s horizon above 0.5 for 3 steps in a row, once the turn has words. Then it flushes, sends `transcript` and runs the turn as usual. The first words of each turn cancel the running turn, as a new press does, and send `state: listening`. The server's turn is often over while the app still plays queued audio, so in this mode `state: listening` is the app's cue to stop playback and drop `audio` until the next `reply`. Each hands-free connection holds an STT session the whole time, even in silence, which counts against Gradium's concurrent session limit.

101	
102	Both directions use Gradium's native format, so the server forwards the base64 strings without decoding them.
103	
104	| Direction | Format | Gradium side |
105	| --- | --- | --- |
106	| Mic, app → server | PCM signed 16-bit little-endian, mono, 24 kHz; 80 ms chunks = 1920 samples = 3840 bytes | STT setup `input_format: "pcm"` |
107	| TTS, server → app | Same format, chunks as Gradium sends them | TTS setup `output_format: "pcm_24000"` (the default `pcm` is 48 kHz) |
108	
109	**iPhone side:** audio session `.playAndRecord` with `.defaultToSpeaker`, or iOS plays through the quiet earpiece while the mic is on. Turn on echo cancellation with `inputNode.setVoiceProcessingEnabled(true)` before reading the input format. Convert the input with `AVAudioConverter` to Int16 at 24 kHz mono. Play through an `AVAudioPlayerNode` on the same engine, converting each chunk to a Float32 24 kHz buffer.
110	
111	**Gradium facts the server relies on** ([docs](https://docs.gradium.ai/api-reference/introduction)): auth header `x-api-key`; STT at `wss://api.gradium.ai/api/speech/asr`, TTS at `wss://api.gradium.ai/api/speech/tts`; the Python SDK is `pip install gradium`. STT needs `json_config.language` (`en` for the demo, `any` to auto-detect). STT sends `text` segments, not partial and final flags. On push-to-talk release the server sends `flush`, waits for `flushed`, and joins the segments into the transcript. TTS has no cancel message: closing the socket stops it.
